decisions.question: Where does the code of the NidanaModule binding land, given that the shell (.6) constructs the executor's route builder and the module observer, the pages and the route builder are .5's files, and .7 is tests only?

options.label: Page wrapper parameter in .5, binding switch and wrapper in .6, both bindings run in .7
options.consequence: No phase edits another's file (D4 holds); .5 grows by a parameter and a small test (about 410 lines), .6 by an enum, a switch and the wrapper (about 410 lines), .7 stays tests only.

options.label: Everything in .7
options.consequence: The wrapper and switch would be written by .7 into .5's route builder and .6's shell, making .7 collide with both and breaking D4's no-shared-file layout.

options.label: .5 owns the wrapper placement and a binding enum in the route builder
options.consequence: .5 would decide the module's pages and grow to about 440 lines, and .6 would still need the switch for the observer.

options.label: NidanaModule inside each checkout page's own build
options.consequence: The pages would hold the module under either binding, so the observer run would also count the wrappers' references; .5's page tests would need a started bus with a module.

decisions.chosen: Page wrapper parameter in .5, binding switch and wrapper in .6, both bindings run in .7
decisions.why: The route builder (.5) owns the entry-to-page mapping and the shell (.6) owns composition choices, so a hook in one and the switch in the other keeps each decision where its file is and keeps D4's rule that no two phases edit one file. Close call against .5 owning the placement; the signal that would have changed my mind: .6 already at its window, which it is not (about 380 lines before).
evidence: hsdd/contract/flutter-binding.md Refinement 8, G20, Not here, Delivery

decisions.question: Where does the example place NidanaModule: around a shell route that hosts the checkout subtree, or in each checkout page?

options.label: In each checkout page, through the route builder
options.consequence: Works with the example's single root Navigator driven by FlutterNavigationExecutor; three wrappers declare one scope (bus-api@v2 G27, flutter-binding@v2 G20); release follows each page's exit transition.

options.label: Around a shell route over a nested Navigator
options.consequence: Needs a nested Navigator for the checkout subtree, which FlutterNavigationExecutor does not drive (one executor per coordination domain, over the root Navigator; flutter-binding@v2 Not here).

decisions.chosen: In each checkout page, through the route builder
decisions.why: Spec §7.3 names both placements; the example has no shell route, and flutter-binding@v2 puts an executor per nested Navigator out of v2, so the per-page placement is the only one the example's navigation supports.

decisions.question: How does the example select between the two module bindings?

options.label: A ModuleBinding enum argument on bootstrapApp, observer by default
options.consequence: One shell, one example app; main runs the observer; tests run either; a closed ADT the switch matches exhaustively.

options.label: Both bindings at once
options.consequence: Wrappers and observer share one scope and add references, so the module's lifetime would be the union of both and neither binding's own lifetime would be tested.

options.label: Two shells
options.consequence: Duplicates the bootstrap composition for one difference.

decisions.chosen: A ModuleBinding enum argument on bootstrapApp, observer by default
decisions.why: The owner's preference for ADTs and composition; the slice needs each binding's lifetime on its own, which only an exclusive choice gives. No evidence beyond the contracts was needed.
evidence: hsdd/contract/flutter-binding.md G10, G20 (shared scope when both declare one module)

decisions.question: Which phase owns the new scope-timing slice (start() before the UI; a MODULE or PAGE binding before start() rejected with a StateError and binding nothing)?

options.label: .7 for the rejections, .6 for main's order
options.consequence: The slice sits with the module and page scopes it rejects; .7 grows to about 380 lines and 8 tasks; .6's main already follows the order.

options.label: All in .6

options.label: Page rejection in .5, module rejection in .7
options.consequence: .5 is a spot-check phase of thin widgets already at about 410 lines; the slice would be split across two phases and two tiers.

decisions.question: Under the observer binding the example never shows a checkout route to the observer before start() (its Navigator mounts after start(), and until then the router's stack holds home alone). How does .7 exercise the module scope's rejection before start() under that binding?

options.label: Acquire the scope the shell's observer declared, before start()
options.consequence: Exercises the call the observer makes at didPush through the example's own declared scope; deterministic; the observer's reporting path stays with flutter-binding@v2's G10 case, which the unrestricted replay runs.

options.label: Mount a Navigator with a checkout initial route before start()
options.consequence: Needs a test-only executor with another initial route, so it would test the adapter's G10 rather than the example's composition.

options.label: Exercise only the wrapper and the page
options.consequence: Leaves the observer binding's half of the slice unproven in the example.

decisions.chosen: Acquire the scope the shell's observer declared, before start()
decisions.why: The Owns slice names 'a module scope's acquire'; the direct acquire is exactly that, on the example's scope. The signal that would have changed my mind: an example flow that mounts the Navigator before start(), which Spec §7.2 tells the app not to do.
evidence: hsdd/contract/flutter-binding.md G10 (the G10 case at fixture line 1183)

decisions.question: Under the wrapper binding the release comes at the end of the popped page's exit transition, later than the observer's. Does the example raise its module grace period to cover MaterialPageRoute's transition, or keep the default?

options.label: Keep the default grace period, count from the release
options.consequence: Both bindings use bus-api@v2's default (100 ms); .7's pumps count from the pop under the observer and from the transition's end under the wrapper, which is the difference the slice should show.

options.label: Raise the grace period to cover the transition
options.consequence: Hides the timing difference between the bindings and departs from the default the contract states.

decisions.chosen: Keep the default grace period, count from the release
decisions.why: flutter-binding@v2 Refinement 3 already says the grace period covers the exit transition for the observer and that a module with a longer transition raises it; the example has no transition-dependent state in the checkout topologies, so the default is safe and the test pins each binding's own release point.

decisions.question: Does .4's bootstrap test check that a service's subscription made during bootstrap is connected by start(), which the restated Owns bootstrap slice names?

options.label: Yes: the payment service receives what a payment request after start() causes
options.consequence: About 10 lines; the restated slice's 'service subscriptions ... connected at start() after the topologies' has a test in the VM lane.

options.label: No: the executor's subscription already shows it
options.consequence: The executor is not a service; the slice's service half would rest on .3's and .6's tests only by accident.

decisions.chosen: Yes: the payment service receives what a payment request after start() causes
decisions.why: Cheap and direct. The request is published after start() on purpose: a request queued before start() behind a LoggedIn would see the pre-login auth.state, because auth-core's publish during step 3 is reentrant (bus-api@v2 G14, G34), which would test reentrancy rather than the connection.

It is what the contract states; flagged only because an adopter queuing dependent events before start() may not expect it.
